newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. hails Angola unity gov't, renews peace force.
newsitem.headline: U.N. hails Angola unity gov't, renews peace force.

text.p: The Security Council warmly welcomed on Wednesday the recent inauguration of a national unity government in Angola and renewed the mandate of the U.N. peacekeeping force there until June 30.

In a unanimous resolution, the council also asked Secretary-General Kofi Annan to complete the withdrawal of U.N. military units, already under way, and called for the start of a transition to a U.N. observer mission.

The peacekeeping force, called the U.N. Angola Verification Mission (UNAVEM III), numbered more than 7,000 at its peak and cost over $300 million a year. It is now down to about 5,500 but is still the biggest U.N. field operation.

It helped implement a 1994 peace accord ending nearly two decades of civil war between the ruling Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), led by President Jose Eduardo dos Santos, and former rebels of the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), headed by Jonas Savimbi.
A highlight of the accord was the inauguration last Friday, after repeated delays, of a government of unity and national reconciliation that includes representatives of both parties.

In an indication of the still uneasy partnership, Savimbi did not attend the inauguration, citing fears for his safety in Luanda, the capital. He has been appoined "president of the largest opposition party," which carries the right to regular consultation with dos Santos and an official residence.
UNITA, which controls diamond-mining areas, has been given the portfolios of geology and mines, tourism, trade and health.

Annan, in a report after a recent visit to Angola, recommended the establishment on July 1 of a U.N. observer mission, whose size he did not specify, to help oversee remaining military provisions of the peace agreement and focus on political, police, human rights, humanitarian and public information issues.
The Security Council said it intended to consider such a follow-on U.N. presence and asked Annan for recommendations by June 6 regarding its structure, goals, and costs.

The council meanwhile strongly urged the Angolan parties to complete the military elements of the accord, including incorporating some UNITA personnel into the Angolan armed forces and national police, demobilizing others, and normalising state administration throughout the country.
The council expressed the hope that a meeting would take place on Angolan territory between dos Santos and Savimbi, as a contribution towards national reconciliation.

Before the council resolution was adopted, numerous speakers, including non-members of the council, praised the establishment of the unity government after years of turmoil and delays. They urged the completion of unfinished business and the consolidation of national reconciliation, aided by a continuing U.N. presence.

Several speakers also expressed concern at recent reports of involvement by the Angolan parties in the crisis in Zaire, whose government in the past helped UNITA. Angolan U.N. envoy Afonso Van Dunem Mbinda, denying his government was involved in Zaire, urged the council to "stick to the Angolan question and leave the question of Zaire as an internal conflict of that country."
The council was presided over by ambassador Antonio Monteiro of Portugal, which ruled Angola before it attained independence in 1975.
